chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah from his father from al-Qasim ibn Ibrahim from Aban ibn Taghlib who said:

I was traveling with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) as his companion between Mecca and Medina. When he reached the Sanctuary (al-Haram), he dismounted, performed ritual bath (ghusl), and took his sandals in his hands with both hands, then entered the Sanctuary barefoot. I did as he did. He said, 'O Aban! Whoever does what I did out of humility for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, Allah will erase a hundred thousand bad deeds from him, record for him a hundred thousand good deeds, build for him a hundred thousand degrees (of reward), and fulfill for him a hundred thousand needs.'

And whoever is unable to perform the bath upon entering the Sanctuary, let him delay it until he is able before entering Mecca. If he is unable, it is permissible for him to perform the bath after entering Mecca.

key_terms.الْحَرَم: The Sanctuary (specifically referring to the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca)
key_terms.دَرَجَةٍ: Degree / Rank (in Paradise or spiritual status)
key_terms.غُسْل: Ritual bath (full body washing for major impurity)

ai.seo_question: What is the reward for entering Mecca barefoot and performing ghusl according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Imami tradition of emulating Imam al-Sadiq’s physical humility by entering the Haram barefoot after purification, a practice distinct from the general Sunnah of wearing shoes. The promise of erasing a hundred thousand sins underscores the theological weight of *tawadhu'* (humility) in Shia jurisprudence, while the ruling on delayed ghusl reflects the practical legal flexibility (*rukhsah*) granted to pilgrims facing logistical constraints.
